pos: adj. (large in magnitude, number, or dignity; rendering Hebrew gadol, rab, Greek megas)
etymology: From Saxon great, thick, coarse, large. The word runs the whole scale of Scripture: a great fish, a great multitude, a great commandment, and a great God — and the Bible never lets the smaller senses erode the greatest.
biblical_def: Great is one of the plainest words in the Authorized Version and one of the most theologically loaded, because Scripture applies it to God first and measures everything else against Him. Moses grounds Israel's obedience in it: “For the LORD your God is God of gods, and Lord of lords, a great God, a mighty, and a terrible, which regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward” (Deuteronomy 10:17). The Psalmist makes the greatness unmeasurable rather than merely large: “Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable” (Psalm 145:3). This is the difference between a superlative and an attribute. A great mountain can be surveyed; a great God cannot, and the confession that His greatness is unsearchable is a confession of creaturely limit, not a compliment. From that fixed point the word orders lesser things. Our Lord ranks the commandments and calls the first one great (Matthew 22:38), which means greatness in the moral realm is assigned by God and not discovered by us. He is Himself named “that great shepherd of the sheep” (Hebrews 13:20), and the office is great because the blood by which He was raised is of infinite worth. Where men are called great in Scripture they are great derivatively — a great nation promised to Abraham, a great name given rather than seized — and where they grasp at greatness directly, as at Babel, the word turns against them.
webster_summary: Large in bulk, number, or dignity; and by extension eminent, illustrious, of high rank. Scripture reserves the unqualified use for God, whose greatness Psalm 145 calls unsearchable, and assigns derived greatness to men and offices as He pleases.
webster_full: GREAT, a. [Sax. great; D. groot; G. gross.] Large in bulk or dimensions; a term of comparison, denoting more magnitude or extension than something else, or beyond what is usual; as a great house; a great river.
2. Large in number; as a great many; a great multitude.
3. Expressing a large, extensive or unusual degree of any thing; as great fear; great love; great pain.
4. Eminent; distinguished; illustrious; as a great hero; a great statesman. Hence, of elevated rank or dignity; noble; magnanimous.

5. Chief; principal; of first importance; as the great commandment. Mat. 22. Applied to God, denoting the infinite excellence and majesty of the divine nature. Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised. Ps. 145.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 10:17
For the LORD your God is God of gods, and Lord of lords, a great God, a mighty, and a terrible, which regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward:
Psalm 145:3
Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable.
Matthew 22:38
This is the first and great commandment.
Hebrews 13:20
Now the God of peace, that brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant,
corruption_summary: Greatness has been detached from God and reassigned to reach — audience, platform, influence — so that a man is called great for the size of the crowd he gathers rather than for the Master he serves.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern account of greatness is quantitative and self-referential: a great leader is one whose following is large, a great ministry is one whose numbers rise, a great life is one that leaves a measurable mark. Every one of those measures can be satisfied without God, and most of them are satisfied best by men who have no fear of Him. Scripture does not merely add a religious qualifier to this scale; it inverts it. “Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” sets the standard where no crowd can see it, and the Lord who said it washed feet. The reversal is not a paradox for devotional effect. It follows from Deuteronomy 10:17: the great God regardeth not persons, which means the very thing that makes a man great in the world's reckoning — that he is a person of consequence, worth regarding — is precisely what God does not weigh.

The second corruption is subtler and works inside the church. Because great is a comparative word, it can be applied to God in a way that only means bigger than the rest, and a God who is merely the largest item in the universe is still an item in it. Psalm 145:3 forbids this: His greatness is unsearchable, not simply unmatched. Recover that and worship changes character. Praise is no longer the awarding of a superlative by a creature competent to judge the field; it is the confession of a greatness that exceeds the instrument measuring it. That is why the same verse pairs greatness with praise and then admits defeat — greatly to be praised, and still unsearchable. The proper end of the word is not flattery but silence, and then obedience.
roots_summary: Hebrew gadol (great, large, elder) and rab (many, much, chief); Greek megas (great in any dimension), polys (much, many), and the comparative meizon our Lord uses to rank greatness in the kingdom.
roots_lines: Hebrew gadol (H1419) — great, large, elder; the word in “a great God” (Deuteronomy 10:17) and “Great is the LORD” (Psalm 145:3).
Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to grow, become great, magnify; the verb behind Abraham's promised great name and behind magnifying the LORD.
Hebrew rab (H7227) — much, many, great in number or rank; often rendered great of a multitude or of a chief officer.
Greek megas (G3173) — great in magnitude, degree, or dignity; the word in “the first and great commandment” (Matthew 22:38).
Greek meizon (G3187) — greater, the comparative of megas; the term in the disciples' dispute over who should be greatest.
usage: “A great God, a mighty, and a terrible” — greatness named together with power and holy dread, not with popularity.
“His greatness is unsearchable” — the attribute exceeds the creature measuring it.
“That great shepherd of the sheep” — the office is great because of the blood that purchased it.

pos: adj. (elevated in place, rank, or dignity; rendering Hebrew rum, gaboah, elyon, Greek hypsistos)
etymology: From Saxon heah, high, tall. In Scripture the word carries a moral charge in both directions: God is the high and lofty One, and the sinner's high look is an abomination — the same height is glory in Him and pride in us.
biblical_def: High in Scripture is first a name for God and only afterward a measurement. He is the most High, and the title governs the whole vocabulary of elevation: “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1). Isaiah gives the fullest statement, and it contains the surprise that keeps the word from becoming mere distance: “For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit” (Isaiah 57:15). The Most High has two addresses, and the second is a broken heart. That is transcendence and condescension held in one verse, and it forbids both the deism that puts God safely above and the sentimentality that brings Him down by lowering Him. In the priesthood the word names the office of the one Mediator: “For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens” (Hebrews 7:26) — separation and exaltation together, since the height is what makes the intercession effectual. Turned toward the creature, high marks the limit of knowledge: “Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it” (Psalm 139:6). And turned toward sin it names idolatry's favourite location, the high places that even good kings failed to remove.
webster_summary: Elevated above the surface, and figuratively exalted in rank, dignity, or degree. Scripture makes it a divine title — the most High — while marking the high look and the high place as the standing shapes of pride and idolatry.
webster_full: HIGH, a. [Sax. heah, heh; G. hoch; D. hoog.] Extending to a great distance above the surface of the earth; elevated; lofty; of great altitude; as a high mountain; a high tower.
2. Elevated in rank, condition, or office; exalted; dignified; as a person of high birth; high in office.
3. Proud; lofty; arrogant; as a high look, which the Scriptures condemn. Prov. 21.
4. Great in degree or intensity; as high winds; high esteem; a high price.

5. Applied to the Supreme Being, the most High, denoting his supremacy over all created things. He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High. Ps. 91. Also, the high places, the elevated spots where idolatrous worship was performed.
scriptures: Psalm 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
Isaiah 57:15

For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones.
Hebrews 7:26
For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens;
Psalm 139:6
Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.
corruption_summary: The height of God has been flattened into friendliness — a God near at hand and nothing else — so that Isaiah's pairing of the high and holy place with the contrite heart is halved, and only the comfortable half is preached.
corruption_paragraphs: A generation taught to speak of God chiefly as friend, companion, and the one who is with us has kept a true thing and lost the thing that made it staggering. Isaiah 57:15 does not begin with nearness; it begins with the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy, and only then adds the second dwelling. Remove the first clause and the second is no longer grace, merely proximity — a God who is near because He was never far, never holy, never a consuming fire. The practical effects are visible in worship that cannot produce reverence, in prayer that has lost the posture of a suppliant, and in a doctrine of sin that cannot explain why a contrite spirit was necessary in the first place. Psalm 139:6 belongs here too: a God whose knowledge is too high for the creature to attain is not a God the creature may edit.

The opposite failure has its own history in Scripture, and the high places are its monument. Israel did not usually abandon the LORD outright; she worshipped Him, and then also kept the elevated shrines, and the historian's refrain over one decent king after another is that the high places were not taken away. That is the enduring pattern of half-reformation: real repentance in the centre, an unrelinquished altar on the hill. The principle to recover is that height belongs to God alone — He is the most High, and every rival elevation, whether a hilltop shrine or a private reservation in the heart, is to be pulled down rather than tolerated. Where the true height is confessed, the false ones lose their attraction; where it is softened, they multiply.
roots_summary: Hebrew elyon (Most High), rum (to be high, lifted up), gaboah (lofty, haughty), and bamah (high place); Greek hypsistos (highest) and hypsos (height, exaltation).
roots_lines: Hebrew elyon (H5945) — Most High; the divine title in Psalm 91:1 and in Melchizedek's priesthood of the most high God.
Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, rise, be lifted up; used of God's exaltation and of the proud high look.
Hebrew gaboah (H1364) — high, lofty, and by extension haughty; the word in “the high and lofty One” register.
Hebrew bamah (H1116) — high place; the elevated shrine repeatedly said not to have been taken away.
Greek hypsistos (G5310) — highest, most high; the title in “Glory to God in the highest” and in the Son of the Highest.
usage: “The secret place of the most High” — the title of supremacy used as the address of refuge.
“I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit” — two dwellings, one God.
“It is high, I cannot attain unto it” — the creature confessing the ceiling of his own knowledge.

pos: adj. & n. (straight, upright, conformed to a rule; also the right hand as the place of power; rendering Hebrew yashar, yamin, Greek orthos, dexios)
etymology: From Saxon riht, straight, direct, akin to Latin rectus. The root idea is a straight line, and every moral use of the word depends on there being a rule straight enough to measure by.
biblical_def: Right in the Authorized Version runs along two lines that meet in Christ. The first is position: the right hand is the place of strength and honour, and the Father assigns it to the Son. “The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool” (Psalm 110:1) — the verse the New Testament quotes more than any other, and Hebrews reports its fulfilment: when He “had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3). The second line is moral: right is what conforms to God's rule, and Scripture is blunt that the creature is not a competent judge of it. The book of Judges closes on the sentence that explains the whole ruin: “In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). Proverbs generalizes it into a warning about sincerity: “There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death” (Proverbs 14:12). Note what is conceded. The way seems right; the man is not lying, he is deceived, and the error is fatal anyway. So the two lines converge: because there is a King at the right hand, there is a rule that is right apart from my eyes — and my eyes are exactly the instrument Scripture says has failed.
webster_summary: Straight, and hence conformed to the standard of truth and justice; also the right hand, the side of power and honour. Judges 21:25 and Proverbs 14:12 both name the same failure — a man judging right by his own eyes.
webster_full: RIGHT, a. [Sax. riht; L. rectus; from the root of rego, to rule, to make straight.] Properly, strait; direct; not crooked; as a right line.
2. Conformable to the will of God, or to his law; just; equitable; not deviating from the standard of moral rectitude. That which is right is holy and good.
3. Conformable to truth; not erroneous; correct in judgment or opinion.
4. Fit; suitable; proper; becoming; as the right man for the office.
5. Denoting the side opposite to the left, and by figure the side of honor and power. Sit thou at my right hand. Ps. 110.
scriptures: Psalm 110:1
A Psalm of David. The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
Judges 21:25
In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
Proverbs 14:12
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
Hebrews 1:3

Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;
corruption_summary: The word has migrated from right as a standard outside the man to rights as a claim asserted by him — and once the plural noun swallows the adjective, Judges 21:25 stops reading as an indictment and starts reading as a description of freedom.
corruption_paragraphs: Two moves accomplish this, and they are usually made without argument. The first replaces conformity to a rule with authenticity to a self: what is right for a man becomes whatever is genuinely his, and the highest sin becomes insincerity rather than transgression. The second turns the moral vocabulary into the language of entitlement, so that public debate is a collision of asserted rights with no standard above them by which any could be adjudicated. Scripture anticipated both. Judges 21:25 is a verdict, not a charter, and the book has just spent five chapters showing what every man doing right in his own eyes actually produces — a mutilated concubine, a civil war, and abducted daughters. Proverbs 14:12 forecloses the appeal to sincerity in advance: the way seemeth right, and the man walking it is not a hypocrite. He is sincere and he is going to die.

The recovery runs through the other sense of the word. There is a right hand, and it is occupied. Psalm 110:1 says a King sits there until His enemies are made His footstool, and Hebrews 1:3 says He sat down because the purging of sins was finished. That is the ground on which the moral sense of right can be held without tyranny: the rule is not an abstraction that crushes, but the will of a King who bled to bring rebels under it. Where that throne is denied, the only available standard is the individual eye, and the culture that results is not free but arbitrary, since a claim asserted can always be out-asserted. Where the throne is confessed, a man may be told he is wrong and live — because the One who tells him has already sat down.
roots_summary: Hebrew yashar (straight, upright, right), yamin (the right hand), and tsedeq (righteousness as conformity to a standard); Greek orthos (straight), dexios (the right hand), dikaios (just, right).
roots_lines: Hebrew yashar (H3477) — straight, upright, right; the word in “right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25) and in doing that which is right in the sight of the LORD.
Hebrew yamin (H3225) — the right hand, the side of strength; the term in Psalm 110:1.
Hebrew tsedeq (H6664) — rightness, justice, righteousness; the standard by which a way is judged right rather than merely felt to be.
Greek dexios (G1188) — right, right hand; used of the Son seated at the right hand of the Majesty (Hebrews 1:3).
Greek orthos (G3717) — straight, erect; the root behind orthotomeo, to divide rightly, in 2 Timothy 2:15.
usage: “Sit thou at my right hand” — the place of power given, not seized.
“Every man did that which was right in his own eyes” — the closing verdict of Judges, not a description of liberty.
“There is a way which seemeth right unto a man” — sincerity conceded, and the end still death.

pos: adj. & pple. (made happy by God; also worthy to be praised; rendering Hebrew ashre, baruk, Greek makarios, eulogetos)
etymology: From Saxon bletsian, to consecrate, anciently connected with blood and the hallowing of an altar. The English word carries two distinct originals in Scripture, and confusing them is the commonest error in reading it.
biblical_def: Blessed translates two different words and points in two different directions, and Scripture never mixes them. When God is the object, the sense is worthy to be praised: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 1:3). Paul is not wishing God well; he is ascribing what is already His, and the same verse then turns the other direction — God blesses us, and the blessings named are spiritual and located in Christ, not in circumstance. Paul carries the ascription further and calls Him “the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings, and Lord of lords” (1 Timothy 6:15). When man is the object, the sense is happy under God's favour, and the Psalter opens with it as a description of a settled life: “Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful” (Psalm 1:1). The blessedness is defined first by what the man refuses. Our Lord takes the same form and drives it to the place no natural reading would go: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3). The blessing is announced over the bankrupt, and the reason given is possession of a kingdom — which is to say blessedness in Scripture is a verdict from heaven upon a man, not a report on his conditions.
webster_summary: Made happy or prosperous by God's favour; and, when applied to God, worthy of adoration and praise. Psalm 1 and the Beatitudes both define the blessed man by his relation to God rather than by his circumstances.
webster_full: BLESSED, pp. Made happy or prosperous; extolled; pronounced happy.
2. a. Happy; prosperous in worldly affairs; enjoying spiritual happiness and the favor of God. Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly. Ps. 1.
3. Happy in heavenly enjoyment; as the blessed in heaven.
4. Worthy of adoration; holy; as the blessed God; the blessed and only Potentate. 1 Tim. 6.
5. It is used in the phrase blessed be, as an ascription of praise, and in blessed are, as a declaration of the happy state of those described. Blessed are the poor in spirit. Mat. 5.
scriptures: Psalm 1:1
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.
Matthew 5:3
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Ephesians 1:3
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ:
1 Timothy 6:15
Which in his times he shall shew, who is the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings, and Lord of lords;
corruption_summary: Blessed has been reduced to a caption for good fortune — the house, the health, the raise — which makes the Beatitudes unreadable, since they pronounce blessing on the poor, the mourning, and the persecuted.
corruption_paragraphs: The word now functions as a tag attached to visible advantage, and the effect is to make blessing evidence. If a man is blessed because his circumstances are favourable, then unfavourable circumstances are evidence of the withdrawal of favour, and the whole apparatus of the prosperity teaching follows by simple logic. Scripture destroys the premise in the first sentence of the Sermon on the Mount. “Blessed are the poor in spirit” is not a promise that the poor in spirit will soon be rich in spirit; it is a declaration that theirs is the kingdom of heaven, present tense, in the condition described. Job in the ash heap is blessed. Paul in the Mamertine is blessed. The Lord Himself, having nowhere to lay His head, is the blessed and only Potentate's beloved Son, and the caption would not have fit Him for a single day of His ministry.

The recovery is to hear the word as a verdict rather than a description. Psalm 1 begins by naming three things the blessed man does not do — he does not walk, stand, or sit with the ungodly, the sinner, and the scorner — and only then says what he delights in. Blessedness is bound to a settled relation to God's law and a settled separation from the counsel of the ungodly, neither of which shows in a photograph. Ephesians 1:3 locates the blessings precisely: all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ. That is where they are kept, and it is why they cannot be lost in a market crash or a diagnosis. A believer who learns to say blessed be God before he says I am blessed has the two senses in the right order, and the second will stop lying to him.
roots_summary: Hebrew ashre (happy, blessed — of man) and barak / baruk (to kneel, to bless — chiefly of God); Greek makarios (blessed, happy — of man) and eulogetos (well-spoken-of, worthy of praise — of God).
roots_lines: Hebrew ashre (H835) — happiness, blessedness of a man; the opening word of the Psalter, “Blessed is the man” (Psalm 1:1).
Hebrew barak (H1288) — to kneel, and so to bless; used both of God blessing man and of man blessing God in adoration.
Greek makarios (G3107) — blessed, happy; the word repeated nine times in the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-11).
Greek eulogetos (G2128) — worthy to be praised, blessed; used in the New Testament of God alone, as in Ephesians 1:3.
Greek eulogeo (G2127) — to speak well of, bless; the verb behind “hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings.”
usage: “Blessed be the God and Father” — ascription to God of what is already His.
“Blessed are the poor in spirit” — the verdict pronounced over the bankrupt, in the condition described.
“All spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ” — the location of the believer's blessing, safe from circumstance.

pos: adj. (empty, worthless, without effect; rendering Hebrew shav, hebel, riq, Greek kenos, mataios)
etymology: From Latin vanus, empty, void. The English sense of conceit is late and secondary; in Scripture the primary idea is emptiness — a thing with the shape of substance and none of the weight.
biblical_def: Vain in Scripture means empty, and the emptiness is usually the gap between what a thing claims and what it delivers. The third commandment forbids attaching God's name to that gap: “Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain” (Exodus 20:7). The prohibition is far wider than profanity. To take the name in vain is to bear it emptily — to swear by it and not perform, to invoke it over what He has not authorized, to be called by it and live as though He were not. The Psalmist applies the same emptiness to labour undertaken without Him: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psalm 127:1). The house may still go up; the point is that the building was hollow. James turns the word on religion itself: “If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain” (James 1:26) — the outward form intact and the content gone. Against all of it stands Paul's resurrection conclusion, which is the one place the word is denied: “forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Because the tomb is empty, the work is not.
webster_summary: Empty, worthless, having no substance or effect; and by extension fruitless, ineffectual. The third commandment forbids bearing God's name emptily, and 1 Corinthians 15:58 is the resurrection's answer to the fear that labour is wasted.
webster_full: VAIN, a. [L. vanus; Fr. vain.] Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance. Why do the people imagine a vain thing? Ps. 2.
2. Fruitless; ineffectual. All attempts, all efforts were vain. Except the Lord build the house, they labor in vain that build it. Ps. 127.
3. Proud of petty things, or of trifling attainments; elated with a high opinion of one's own accomplishments.
4. Empty; unreal; as a vain show; a vain imagination.
5. In vain, to no purpose; without effect; ineffectually. To take the name of God in vain, is to use it wantonly, irreverently, or in a false oath. Ex. 20.
scriptures: Exodus 20:7
Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
Psalm 127:1
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
James 1:26
If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain.
1 Corinthians 15:58
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
corruption_summary: The third commandment has been shrunk to a rule about swear words, which leaves the far commoner sin untouched — the empty bearing of God's name by people who invoke it over plans He never authorized.
corruption_paragraphs: Where in vain is heard as as a curse word, the commandment costs almost nothing, and a man may keep it perfectly while attaching the name of God to his ambitions every week. The Hebrew shav means emptiness, falsehood, worthlessness; the prohibition is against carrying the name without weight. That reaches the oath not performed, the prophecy claimed and unfulfilled, the cause advertised as God's that is merely ours, and — most searchingly — the profession of the name by a life that contradicts it. The clause attached to the commandment is unusual and should be felt: the LORD will not hold him guiltless. Of the ten, this is the one that specifically forecloses the assumption that the offence is minor.

James supplies the domestic test and it is not the one most would choose. A man may seem to be religious — attendance, vocabulary, sincerity all intact — and if he does not bridle his tongue his religion is vain, empty, the same word. The tongue is chosen because it is the organ by which the name is most often borne, and the least guarded. Psalm 127 gives the constructive side: work is not vain because it is small or unnoticed, but because it is undertaken apart from the LORD who builds and keeps. And 1 Corinthians 15:58 removes the fear from the other direction. Paul has just finished arguing the resurrection, and the practical conclusion he draws is not about heaven but about Monday: be stedfast, unmoveable, abounding, because your labour is not in vain in the Lord. Emptiness is the default of everything done outside Him and impossible for anything done in Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew shav (emptiness, falsehood — the word in the third commandment), hebel (vapour, vanity — Ecclesiastes), and riq (emptiness); Greek kenos (empty) and mataios (futile, purposeless).
roots_lines: Hebrew shav (H7723) — emptiness, vanity, falsehood; the term in “take the name of the LORD thy God in vain” (Exodus 20:7).
Hebrew hebel (H1892) — vapour, breath, vanity; the refrain of Ecclesiastes, vanity of vanities.
Hebrew riq (H7385) — emptiness, to no purpose; used of labour and of imagining a vain thing.
Greek kenos (G2756) — empty, without content; Paul's word for a faith and a preaching that would be vain if Christ be not raised.
Greek mataios (G3152) — futile, purposeless, ineffectual; the word behind the vain religion of James 1:26.
usage: “Take the name of the LORD thy God in vain” — to bear the name emptily, far wider than profanity.
“They labour in vain that build it” — the house may rise and still be hollow.
“Your labour is not in vain in the Lord” — the one denial of emptiness, grounded in the resurrection.

pos: adj. (filled, containing all it can hold; rendering Hebrew male, Greek pleres, with the noun pleroma, fulness)
etymology: From Saxon ful, akin to Latin plenus. Scripture's decisive uses are not about quantity but about what fills — grace and truth, the Holy Ghost, the Godhead bodily.
biblical_def: Full in Scripture is almost always answered by the question full of what, and the answers are the doctrine. John says of the incarnate Word that He “dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Both together, and neither diluted by the other — a fulness of grace that does not soften truth, a fulness of truth that does not withhold grace. Paul presses further and states the deity without remainder: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Colossians 2:9). All the fulness, and bodily; the verse is the standing refutation of every scheme that makes Christ a partial vessel of deity or a temporary one. From the Head the word descends to the members. The qualification the apostles required for the first deacons was not administrative: “look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Acts 6:3) — the plainest table service in the church demanded men who were full. And our Lord makes fulness a matter of the eye and therefore of the whole man: “if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light” (Matthew 6:22). Fulness, in every case, is received rather than generated; a vessel does not fill itself, and the whole biblical usage assumes a giver standing outside the container.
webster_summary: Replete; having within all that the space will contain. Scripture's weight falls on the contents — full of grace and truth, full of the Holy Ghost, and in Christ all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
webster_full: FULL, a. [Sax. ful; L. plenus.] Replete; having within its limits all that it can contain; as a vessel full of water.
2. Abounding with; having a large supply or abundance; as a house full of furniture; a land full of corn.
3. Complete; entire; not defective or partial; as a full account; the full assurance of faith.
4. Saturated; having the mind or heart occupied; as full of thought; full of grace and truth. John 1.
5. Adequate; sufficient; as full satisfaction. Fulness, n. the state of being filled; completeness. In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. Col. 2.
scriptures: John 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Colossians 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
Acts 6:3
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
Matthew 6:22
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
corruption_summary: Fulness has been turned inward and renamed fulfilment — a life that feels complete — so that the biblical question full of what is answered with myself, and the vessel is asked to supply its own contents.
corruption_paragraphs: The promise of a full life is everywhere, and it is almost always a promise about the self: potential realized, purpose discovered, the authentic person finally at home in his own skin. Scripture uses the same adjective and never once locates the contents inside the container. Men are full of the Holy Ghost, full of faith and power, full of goodness and knowledge; the Word made flesh is full of grace and truth; the Godhead dwells in Christ bodily. In every case something has come in from outside. This is not a quibble about phrasing — it decides what a man does when he feels empty. Told that fulness is latent within, he will search himself, and find that the search itself is the emptiness. Told that fulness is given, he will ask, and Christ's standing offer is to the thirsty rather than to the resourceful.

The second distortion is quantitative — the idea that fulness is a matter of more, and that the Christian life is measured in volume of activity. Acts 6:3 corrects it in an unexpected place. The office being filled is the distribution of food to widows, and the requirement is men full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom. The apostles did not scale the qualification to the visibility of the task. And Matthew 6:22 explains the mechanism: fulness of light in the whole body follows from a single eye — an undivided aim. So the road to fulness is not accumulation but singleness, which is why the divided man is always the empty one, and why the remedy Scripture prescribes for emptiness is repentance rather than enrichment.
roots_summary: Hebrew male (to fill, be full); Greek pleres (full), pleroo (to fill, fulfil), and pleroma (fulness, that which fills) — the noun Paul uses of the Godhead in Christ and of the church as His body.
roots_lines: Hebrew male (H4390) — to fill, be full, accomplish; used of the glory filling the tabernacle and of days being fulfilled.
Greek pleres (G4134) — full, complete; the word in “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14) and “full of the Holy Ghost” (Acts 6:3).
Greek pleroma (G4138) — fulness, that which fills; used of the Godhead dwelling bodily in Christ (Colossians 2:9).
Greek pleroo (G4137) — to fill, complete, fulfil; the verb behind being filled with the Spirit and with the knowledge of His will.
Greek haplous (G573) — single, simple, without fold; the eye of Matthew 6:22 whose singleness fills the body with light.
usage: “Full of grace and truth” — both at once, neither diluting the other.
“All the fulness of the Godhead bodily” — deity without remainder, in a body.
“Full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” — the qualification for waiting on tables.

pos: adj. (recently made or come into being; also fresh in kind, of a different quality; rendering Hebrew chadash, Greek kainos and neos)
etymology: From Saxon niwe, akin to Latin novus. The Greek preserves a distinction English has lost: neos, new in time, and kainos, new in kind — and Scripture's great promises use the second.
biblical_def: The Bible's new is not chiefly the recent; it is the qualitatively other, brought in by God where the old had failed. Jeremiah announces it as a covenant: “Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah” (Jeremiah 31:31) — new not because the God who gives it has changed His mind, but because it is written on hearts and secures what the old exposed. Ezekiel states the mechanism: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). The verbs are all His — give, put, take away, give — and the recipient contributes the stone. Paul applies it to the individual in Christ: “Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). The Greek is kainos: not a repaired man but a new kind of man, and the tense of are become forbids treating it as an aspiration. The line closes at the end of the canon with the throne speaking: “Behold, I make all things new” (Revelation 21:5). Note what is not said. He does not say I make all new things; He makes the things that are — heaven, earth, body, city — new. Redemption renews the creation rather than replacing it.
webster_summary: Lately made, or of a fresh kind; not old. Scripture's use is qualitative — a new covenant, a new heart, a new creature, and at last all things made new by the One on the throne.
webster_full: NEW, a. [Sax. niwe; L. novus.] Lately made, invented, produced, or come into being; that has existed a short time only.
2. Lately introduced to our knowledge; not before known; recently discovered; as a new metal; a new country.
3. Different from the former; as a new dress; a new mode of life.
4. Not habituated; unaccustomed; as new to the business. Also, renovated; repaired; as a new heart. Ezek. 36.
5. Recently commenced; as the new year. New covenant, the covenant of grace established through Christ, in distinction from the old or legal dispensation. Jer. 31; Heb. 8.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 5:17
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
Ezekiel 36:26
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
Jeremiah 31:31
Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:
Revelation 21:5
And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new. And he said unto me, Write: for these words are true and faithful.
corruption_summary: Novelty has been made a credential — what is newer is assumed truer — and the church borrows the assumption when it announces a “new thing God is doing” that happens to relieve it of an old command.
corruption_paragraphs: The age holds, mostly without arguing for it, that later is better: a newer ethic supersedes an older one, and a doctrine is refuted by being dated. Inside the church this appears as an appeal to what God is doing now, offered as a reason to stop doing what He said then. The appeal is answered by the very texts it borrows from. The new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31 is new precisely in that the law is written in their hearts — the same law, relocated, not repealed. Ezekiel's new heart is given so that the recipient will “walk in my statutes.” Newness in Scripture always intensifies obedience and never dissolves it. Any proposed new thing whose practical effect is that an old command may now be set aside is not the biblical kainos; it is the oldest thing there is, and it was first proposed in a garden.

The opposite error deserves naming too, because a dictionary in this voice is more likely to be tempted by it: the reflex that treats age as proof and receives whatever is inherited without examination. Scripture is not conservative in that sense. It announced a new covenant, and the men most confident in the old were the ones who crucified its Mediator. The test is neither the calendar nor the tradition but the Word, and by that test the truly new thing is always a work of God on the inside — a heart of flesh where a stone was. Revelation 21:5 sets the horizon: the One on the throne makes all things new, and the sentence immediately following is a command to write, because the newness is announced in words that were true and faithful before the renewal arrived.
roots_summary: Hebrew chadash (new, fresh, and the verb to renew); Greek kainos (new in kind or quality) as distinct from neos (new in time), with anakainoo, to renew inwardly.
roots_lines: Hebrew chadash (H2319) — new, fresh; the adjective in “a new covenant” (Jeremiah 31:31) and “a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
Hebrew chadash as verb (H2318) — to renew, repair; the plea of Psalm 51, renew a right spirit within me.
Greek kainos (G2537) — new in kind, of a different quality; the word in new creature, new covenant, new heaven and new earth.
Greek neos (G3501) — new in point of time, young; used of new wine and of the younger, not of the new creation.
Greek anakainoo (G341) — to renew, make new again; the inward man renewed day by day in 2 Corinthians 4:16.
usage: “A new heart also will I give you” — every verb belongs to God; the man supplies the stone.
“He is a new creature” — kainos, a new kind of man, not a repaired one.
“Behold, I make all things new” — the existing creation renewed, not discarded for other things.

pos: adj. & pple. (affected by shame; put to confusion; rendering Hebrew bosh, Greek aischynomai and epaischynomai)
etymology: From Saxon gescamod, the past participle of scamian, to shame. Scripture uses it in three directions at once — the shame a man ought to feel, the shame he must not feel, and the shame God declines to feel over His own.
biblical_def: Scripture never treats shame as a single thing to be either embraced or eliminated; it sorts it. There is a shame the believer must refuse. “For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth” (Romans 1:16) — and Paul writes it to the capital of the world, where the message of a crucified Jew was contemptible. He grounds the refusal not in confidence about himself but in knowledge of another: “nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day” (2 Timothy 1:12). The object of the knowledge is a person, not a proposition, and that is why the chains did not shame him. There is also a shame a man should fear, and it is tied to work rather than feeling: “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). The remedy prescribed is labour in the text. And there is the most astonishing use of all, where God is the subject: of the pilgrims who desired a better country, “God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:16). He might have been; the text concedes the possibility by denying it, and the reason given is not their worthiness but His preparation.
webster_summary: Affected by shame; abashed or confused by guilt, or by a consciousness of some impropriety. Scripture divides the word sharply — not ashamed of the gospel, needing not to be ashamed as a workman, and God Himself not ashamed to be called their God.
webster_full: ASHAMED, a. [Sax. gescamod, from scamian, to shame.] Affected by shame; abashed or confused by guilt or a conviction of some criminal action or indecorous conduct.
2. Confused by a consciousness of inferiority, of mistake, or of anything derogatory to reputation. They shall be ashamed that transgress without cause. Ps. 25.
3. Followed by of before the object; as ashamed of his conduct. I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ. Rom. 1.
4. Restrained by fear of shame; as, he was ashamed to ask.
5. It is used with a negative to express confidence or boldness. A workman that needeth not to be ashamed. 2 Tim. 2. God is not ashamed to be called their God. Heb. 11.
scriptures: Romans 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
2 Timothy 1:12

For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.
2 Timothy 2:15
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Hebrews 11:16
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
corruption_summary: Shame has been reclassified wholesale as an injury — always a wound inflicted, never a signal of guilt — so that the shame Scripture says a man ought to feel over sin is treated as the sickness, and repentance is prescribed for the wrong patient.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic account divides guilt from shame and then dismisses the second entirely: guilt says I did wrong, shame says I am wrong, and shame is therefore a distortion to be dismantled. There is real pastoral insight buried in the distinction, and Scripture does address the man crushed by a shame that Christ has already borne. But the wholesale verdict is false to the text. The Bible repeatedly rebukes those who could not blush, and treats the loss of shame as an advanced stage of hardening rather than as health. A conscience that no longer colours is not healed; it is cauterized. The proper cure for shame over sin is not to revalue the feeling but to deal with the sin at the cross, after which the shame has no fuel and departs honestly rather than being argued away.

The correction runs in both directions, and Scripture is more demanding than the culture on each. It forbids a shame the modern account would permit — embarrassment at the gospel, which Paul renounces in the one city where renouncing it cost the most, and which today is felt most sharply at the points where Scripture contradicts the age. And it commands a shame the modern account has abolished, the workman's fear of being found unapproved, which 2 Timothy 2:15 answers with study rather than with self-acceptance. Over both stands Hebrews 11:16. God is not ashamed to be called the God of pilgrims with nothing to show, because He has prepared their city. That is where the believer's shame finally goes: not talked out of him, but out-weighed by a Name that has consented to be joined to his.
roots_summary: Hebrew bosh (to be ashamed, put to confusion) and kalam (to be humiliated, disgraced); Greek aischyno (to be ashamed), epaischynomai (to be ashamed of, with an object), and kataischyno (to put to shame).
roots_lines: Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, disappointed, put to confusion; the frequent Psalm plea, let me not be ashamed.
Hebrew kalam (H3637) — to be humiliated, wounded in honour; used where shame is inflicted by an enemy or by disgrace.
Greek epaischynomai (G1870) — to be ashamed of something or someone; the verb Paul negates in Romans 1:16 and 2 Timothy 1:12, and used of God in Hebrews 11:16.
Greek anepaischyntos (G422) — not needing to be ashamed; the single word behind the workman of 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek kataischyno (G2617) — to put to shame, dishonour; hope maketh not ashamed in Romans 5:5.
usage: “I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ” — written to Rome, where the message was contemptible.
“A workman that needeth not to be ashamed” — the remedy prescribed is study in the text, not self-acceptance.
“God is not ashamed to be called their God” — the possibility conceded and denied, on the ground of what He prepared.

pos: v. (to comprehend, perceive the meaning of; rendering Hebrew bin, sakal, Greek syniemi, noeo)
etymology: From Saxon understandan, literally to stand under or among — and the etymology is unusually apt, since Scripture makes understanding a posture beneath the Word rather than a mastery over it.
biblical_def: Understanding in Scripture is a gift before it is an achievement, and the Bible is candid about why it must be. Paul's indictment leaves no exception: “There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God” (Romans 3:11). That is not a comment on intelligence; the men in view are as clever as any. The failure is moral and the organ is darkened, so the reversal must come from outside. Luke reports it happening: “Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luke 24:45). The risen Christ does not merely explain the text to the disciples — He opens the faculty, and only then does the exposition land. The Psalmist therefore asks rather than assumes, and ties the request to obedience: “Give me understanding, and I shall keep thy law; yea, I shall observe it with my whole heart” (Psalm 119:34). Understanding is sought in order to keep, which rules out the notion of a comprehension that leaves conduct untouched. And Nehemiah shows the ordinary means God uses: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). Read clearly, explained, applied — the pattern of preaching, and the reason the church has ministers. The sovereign opening of Luke 24 and the plain teaching of Nehemiah 8 are not rivals; the second is how the first usually arrives.
webster_summary: To comprehend; to have just and adequate ideas of. Scripture holds both that none understands by nature (Romans 3:11) and that Christ opens the understanding (Luke 24:45), with reading and exposition as the ordinary means (Nehemiah 8:8).
webster_full: UNDERSTAND, v.t. [Sax. understandan; under and standan, to stand.] To have just and adequate ideas of; to comprehend; to know; as, to understand a problem.
2. To have the same ideas as the person who speaks, or the ideas which a speaker intends to communicate. I understand the preacher.
3. To receive or comprehend the meaning of a writing or discourse. They gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. Neh. 8.
4. To suppose to mean; to interpret; as, in what sense are we to understand this passage?
5. To learn; to be informed. Understanding, n. the faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things presented to it. Then opened he their understanding. Luke 24.
scriptures: Romans 3:11
There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God.
Luke 24:45
Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,
Psalm 119:34
Give me understanding, and I shall keep thy law; yea, I shall observe it with my whole heart.
Nehemiah 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Understanding has been relocated from the text to the reader — what a passage means becomes what it means to me — which quietly makes every reading equally valid and therefore makes correction impossible.
corruption_paragraphs: The move is often made in a devotional key and sounds humble: who am I to say what it means? But the effect is the opposite of humility. If meaning is supplied by the reader, then the text can never rebuke him, because it can never say anything he did not already put there. Nehemiah 8:8 assumes the contrary at every point. The Levites read distinctly — the words have a fixed shape; they gave the sense — there is a sense to give; they caused them to understand — understanding can be conveyed from one person to another, which is impossible if it is private by nature. The people then wept, which is what happens when a text you did not author tells you something about yourself.

The opposite failure is rationalism, and Romans 3:11 forecloses it just as firmly. The natural man does not lack data; he lacks the faculty, and no amount of scholarship repairs a darkened understanding. This is why Luke 24:45 is such a relief. Christ opened their understanding, and the men whose eyes He opened had walked with Him for three years and still not seen it. Understanding is therefore something to be prayed for before it is studied for, which is exactly the order of Psalm 119:34 — give me understanding, and then I shall keep. A reader who prays that prayer honestly has already surrendered the modern premise, because he has admitted that the meaning is out there, that it is not in his gift, and that when it comes he intends to obey it.
roots_summary: Hebrew bin (to discern, understand) and its noun binah, with sakal (to be prudent, act wisely); Greek syniemi (to put together, comprehend), synesis (understanding), and noeo (to perceive with the mind).
roots_lines: Hebrew bin (H995) — to separate mentally, discern, understand; the verb behind Nehemiah 8:8 and the Psalmist's plea for understanding.
Hebrew binah (H998) — understanding, discernment; paired with wisdom throughout Proverbs and asked for rather than assumed.
Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to be prudent, have insight, act wisely; understanding shown in conduct rather than in speech alone.
Greek syniemi (G4920) — to bring together, and so to comprehend; the word negated in Romans 3:11, “none that understandeth.”
Greek dianoia (G1271) — the mind, the understanding as a faculty; the organ Christ opened in Luke 24:45.
usage: “There is none that understandeth” — the failure is moral, not intellectual.
“Then opened he their understanding” — the faculty opened first, and then the scriptures land.
“Gave the sense, and caused them to understand” — the pattern of preaching, and the reason for a ministry.

pos: adj. (small in size, quantity, or degree; rendering Hebrew qaton, me'at, Greek mikros, oligos)
etymology: From Saxon lytel, small. Scripture uses the word as a term of tenderness (little children, little flock), of rebuke (little faith), and of method (here a little, and there a little) — and all three assume God does not despise the small.
biblical_def: Little in Scripture is rarely a dismissal. Our Lord makes smallness the condition of entry: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3). What is required is not the innocence of children, which they do not have, but their dependence, which they cannot hide. The word is also the Shepherd's address to a frightened congregation: “Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). The two halves of that verse should be held together — a flock small enough to be afraid, and a kingdom given because it pleased the Father to give it. Nothing in the transaction depends on the size of the flock. There is a rebuking use as well: “Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?” (Matthew 8:26). The faith is real, or He would not call it faith; it is little, and littleness of faith shows itself in fear during storms rather than in doctrinal error during calm. Finally the word describes God's ordinary pedagogy: “precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little” (Isaiah 28:10). Even where Isaiah reports it as the mockery of drunkards imitating a prophet's plodding speech, the method stands — God teaches His people in small increments, and the men who found it tedious were destroyed by what they would not learn slowly.
webster_summary: Small in size, quantity, or degree; and by extension slight or of small dignity. Scripture makes littleness the posture of entry into the kingdom, the description of a flock given a kingdom anyway, and the measure of a faith that fears in storms.
webster_full: LITTLE, a. [Sax. lytel; D. luttel.] Small in size or extent; not great or large; as a little body; a little animal.
2. Short in duration; as a little time; a little while.
3. Small in quantity or amount; as a little food; here a little, and there a little. Is. 28.
4. Of small dignity, power or importance. When thou wast little in thine own sight. 1 Sam. 15.
5. Slight; inconsiderable; as a little faith. O ye of little faith. Mat. 8. Little ones, young children; used also of the humble and dependent whom Christ forbids to offend.
scriptures: Matthew 18:3
And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
Luke 12:32
Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
Matthew 8:26
And he saith unto them, Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm.
Isaiah 28:10
For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little:
corruption_summary: An age that measures everything by scale has made littleness a problem to be solved — the small church, the small family, the unnoticed obedience — when Scripture makes it the ordinary shape of the kingdom's work.
corruption_paragraphs: The pressure is felt most by pastors of small congregations and by fathers of ordinary households, and it is rarely stated as doctrine because it does not have to be. It arrives as a metric: attendance, reach, growth rate, the assumption that a faithful work will visibly enlarge and that one which does not has failed. Luke 12:32 is addressed to exactly this fear. The flock is little — Christ concedes the size rather than disputing it — and the kingdom is given not because the flock has grown but because it is the Father's good pleasure. A man who believes that verse can labour thirty years in a village and die without a metric to show, and have lost nothing. A man who does not will eventually change his message to fill his room.

The corresponding discipline is Isaiah 28:10, and it cuts against impatience in the same way. God builds by precept upon precept and line upon line, here a little and there a little — catechism, family worship, the same commands repeated to the same children, the Lord's Day arriving again. This is the method the mockers in Isaiah found risible, and it is the method that raises a household in the faith. The principle to recover is that in the kingdom the small is not the preliminary stage of the large; it is the unit of the work. A mustard seed, a cup of cold water, a widow's two mites, five loaves — the pattern is unbroken, and it is always the Lord who supplies the increase, which is precisely why the size of what He is given has never been the point.
roots_summary: Hebrew qaton (small, young, insignificant) and me'at (a little, few); Greek mikros (small), oligos (few, little), and the compound oligopistos, of little faith.
roots_lines: Hebrew qaton (H6996) — small, young, of no account; used of the least in a household and of Saul when he was little in his own sight.
Hebrew me'at (H4592) — a little, few, a small quantity; the word in “here a little, and there a little” (Isaiah 28:10).
Greek mikros (G3398) — small in size, age, or rank; the term behind the little ones Christ forbids His people to offend.
Greek oligos (G3641) — few, little, small; used of the little flock and of the few who find the narrow way.
Greek oligopistos (G3640) — of little faith; a compound our Lord alone uses, and always of disciples, never of unbelievers.
usage: “Become as little children” — the dependence required, not an innocence children do not have.
“Fear not, little flock” — the size conceded, the kingdom given anyway.
“Here a little, and there a little” — God's ordinary pace in teaching His people.
